EICMA 2026 • Triumph TF-E Bikes Get Even More Enduro With Updates for the 2027 Model Year
Don't Count on Tesla To Deliver Those $59,990 Cybertrucks, As Musk Foreshadows "Amazing Scarcity"
6 photos
Photo: Tesla
Elon Musk announced the demise of the Tesla Cybertruck while at the same time saying that a new shift will be added to its production line. He also said that Tesla "will have to return deposits to a lot of people." Given the recent price hikes and the fact that Tesla doesn't accept new orders on the base variant, it's almost certain that people who ordered it at $59,990 won't get their vehicles.
When Elon Musk turned his back on electric vehicles and Tesla's mission to electrify the transportation sector, he promised the change would bring "amazing abundance." It was March 2025, Musk was the acting DOGE chief, and Tesla sales suffered. As he has often done, Musk deflected criticism by announcing a new direction for the company, one that prioritizes robots, artificial intelligence, and autonomous driving.
More than that, Musk proclaimed that in a not-so-distant future, money would become irrelevant, precisely because robots would do all the work and people would just sit back and enjoy said abundance. Despite that promise, Musk did everything to ensure more money for himself, including a multi-billion compensation package.
Even more, he directed Tesla away from vehicle manufacturing because it did not make enough money and would needlessly consume Tesla's engineering and financial resources. He persistently bragged about trillions in potential revenue generated by Tesla's Robotaxi arm, as if money suddenly mattered again.
The Cybertruck is making money, but somehow disappoints Musk That's the background against which Musk announced that the Cybertruck would stop production in eight months. The announcement caused quite a stir in the Tesla community, even though the electric pickup truck sold in insignificant numbers. The Cybertruck's demise was long anticipated, yet the announcement sent ripples throughout the automotive industry.
The small sales numbers for a vehicle whose development likely cost billions hint at huge losses. However, Musk was quick to point out that the Cybertruck was still profitable. However, he said that building the Cybercab instead would create a lot more value for the company. Coming from the man who said money won't matter soon, this is strange.
Even worse, the way things turned out leaves little hope that those who ordered the cheapest Cybertruck variant would ever get their vehicles. In the same tweet, Musk announced that the Cybertruck's order rate far exceeds the production rate, and a lot of people won't get the vehicle they ordered.
This raises more questions, as Tesla published every quarter in its shareholder decks that the Cybertruck production line has an annual capacity of 125,000 vehicles. This means that it could theoretically build over 80,000 Cybertrucks in the remaining eight months until production stops. If this doesn't sound impressive, you should know that this is more trucks than Tesla has sold since delivery started in November 2023.
That's the same nonsense that Tesla has been fanning since the $59,990 Cybertruck variant went on sale in February. The company pushed delivery estimates into 2027 as if it already exhausted all production slots for 2026. However, as delivery numbers were reported quarter after quarter, we learned that Tesla never sold more than 8,000 trucks per quarter, versus the 30k-unit theoretical production capacity.
The $59,990 Cybertruck is as good as dead There's no reason to believe it will be any different this time. Despite Musk's pledge that Tesla will "try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months," we will undoubtedly see in the following quarters that Tesla only delivered a handful of pickups. Unsurprisingly, he tries to prepare us for this outcome, saying that Tesla "will have to return deposits for a lot of people."
You can argue that Tesla will still make some Cybertrucks, possibly even some of those elusive $59,990 AWD models. Fair point, but let's not forget that the company also raised the prices significantly just last week. Even the base variant, which you can no longer order, is listed with an $82,490 starting price. If you think Tesla would sell you that same truck at $59,990 just because you reserved one in February, I have a bridge to sell.
Even if Tesla does deliver the base Cybertruck AWD to some of the early reservation holders at the price they ordered, it will not make any efforts to prioritize them. In the best-case scenario, some lucky chaps will get their trucks so that they can brag about it on social media.
This actually happened already, with some having received their $59,990 trucks this summer, while others have been put on hold indefinitely. Meanwhile, more expensive variants of the Cybertruck had no restrictions.
This shows that Tesla is reluctantly selling the Cybertruck, and has been doing it all along. Production capacity hasn't been a problem, and the company is no longer constrained by Li-ion cell availability. Even when it promised a cheaper variant that appeared to be successful, it refused to actually build it, blaming huge demand and raising prices instead.
Prepare for a day when you won't be able to buy a Tesla The Cybertruck was not the first Tesla model to go to the graveyard of automotive history. The Model S and Model X were killed just a few months ago. These were also low-volume vehicles, and their demise was entirely justified. This means that Tesla is essentially selling only two vehicle models: the Model 3 and Model Y.
Both have grown long in the tooth, sharing a platform that debuted with the Model 3 in 2017. Despite a recent refresh, they have failed to catch up with Chinese rivals in terms of charging performance and battery tech. It might not matter much in North America. Still, in all other markets, Tesla is slowly but surely falling behind competition.
This has always been a recipe for disaster, and staying on this path will only mean that Model 3 and Model Y will soon disappear, too. That would be the end of Tesla's automotive business, if we don't count the Cybercab. However, the golden driverless car is unlikely to conquer the world despite Musk's optimism.
Even in the most optimistic scenario, the Cybercab will be confined to big cities in the US, with heavy regulatory constraints in other regions. Tesla couldn't push FSD in China, and it won't be able to sell the Cybercab there. Europe might be easier, but not with the current "move fast, break things" attitude. However, the vast majority of people on Earth will still want to drive their own vehicles, and Tesla won't have anything to offer them.
